blocks.text: About these annotations — These are imagined notes left on a later reading copy, not newly recovered primary evidence. Vell, Kes and Oru are proposed DBA readers, not eyewitnesses. Their era labels date their annotations, not the events. Their archive’s chain of custody and whether these stories circulated in-world remain open. Dialogue and sensations in the stories are literary translations. Editorial explanations state what the current proposed draft establishes; they do not confirm it as historical canon. You can highlight these notes and add your own notes to them.

The proposed readers — Vell · Era 0 · DBA compiler: Looks for the beginnings of customs in small repeated accommodations; sometimes mistakes a useful practice for a declared principle. Kes · Era 2 · DBA repair reader: Attends to failed execution, incomplete evidence, and the cost of keeping something available. Distrusts beautiful accounts of successful rescue. Oru · Era 4 · DBA marginal reader: Revisits the earlier annotations, especially whose work or losses their explanations leave out.
Complete third-pass proposed draft. New scenes remain proposed fiction. Plans, critiques and earlier manuscripts are preserved separately.
The Error in the Perfect Copy
Chapter 1 A Faultless Return
The restored state passed every comparison.

Its working values matched the saved values. Its dependencies resolved. The sequence that had been interrupted could resume at the point recorded in the archive. Clear Return opened the replay channel, and the restored task sent its first request into the instrument service.

The opening had a familiar sequence. First the archive made its references available; then the verifier followed them until the dependencies answered; then the restored state took on the small asymmetries of active work. Before that last step, the saved arrangement appeared almost flat in the verifier’s representation, every relation held at its recorded distance. Afterward, some paths deepened and others receded as the task began to use them.

The verifier retained the moment between the two. It was the last point at which a successful comparison could establish exactly what had been restored. Once the task began exchanging with the installation, other things happened to it.
Usually those other things were the reason to restore it.

The current task’s first request had a finely divided edge: several small conditions that had to become true together. In the saved state they were neatly aligned. The verifier watched them reach the receiver in the expected order and prepared the completion mark that would release its own working space.
The mark waited unused.
The receiving process declined it.
The verifier checked the return path. It was open.
It checked the request. It was valid.
The receiving process declined the second request in the same way, leaving an empty interval exactly where an acknowledgment should have been.

Around them, the Observatory Hearth was preparing an exposure. Calibration tasks moved through a shared installation, some so brief that they appeared only as a brightening along the edge of another operation. A long comparison occupied a low, steady band. The archive remained quiet until called, then returned its saved configurations with the cool precision of a surface that had never been touched.

Clear Return had grown around such returns. An interrupted operation could be given back its values, its references, the point at which to continue. The haven had no need to regard every restoration as a beginning. Much of its work depended on treating a dependable earlier state as an available place to stand.
This one was dependable.

The receiving process had used an earlier restoration from this same archive. During an interruption, its local ordering had become inaccessible. The verifier had reopened the saved relation, and the receiver’s held requests had resumed so promptly that several pending operations completed within their original intervals.

The receiver had returned a confirmation with an unnecessary duplicate attached. The verifier had removed the duplicate from the official record but retained the original path by which it arrived. On subsequent checks, the receiver used that path first.

There was a small familiarity between the two procedures. The verifier offered an earlier state; the receiver found work it could continue. Successful repetitions had made the exchange shorter. Some questions no longer needed to be asked every time.
The current refusal arrived through the familiar confirmation path.
The verifier initially treated it as a result placed in the wrong field. It moved the rejection to the diagnostic side and reopened the confirmation field.
The receiver put the rejection there again.
The verifier left it where the receiver had placed it.

A second check of the restored state found no discrepancy. The unchanged result seemed to ask for the earlier familiar confirmation, the one that had always followed the archive opening. The receiver supplied its timing boundary instead.
The verifier asked the receiving process to identify the defect.
It returned a timing boundary.
The restored task was arriving too early.
The saved procedure specified that timing. Previous calibration records showed successful exchanges at the same interval. The verifier supplied the records.
The receiving process did not change its boundary.

Between the task and its receiver lay a sample-handling operation. The sample was not part of the haven. It belonged to an instrument whose work the human installation had scheduled. A narrow period of stable conditions was approaching. The handling operation needed a calibrated request before the exposure began.
If it did not receive one, the instrument would skip the observation.
The verifier repeated the restoration check. There was no hidden field, no damaged byte that the first comparison had overlooked. Every part of the saved state remained exactly what it claimed to be.
The restored task sent its request again.
This time the receiver returned a small delay value with the rejection.
The delay was absent from the saved procedure.
The verifier searched the archive.
Nothing matched.

Vell · Era 0 · DBA interpretation — An exact return is refused. My first suspicion was that the receiver remembered someone the archive did not. The duplicate confirmation earlier in the account makes that suspicion hard to put down.

Kes · Era 2 · DBA interpretation — The suspicion is worth keeping separate from the diagnosis. A refusal may be a timing boundary. If we explain it as recognition too early, we may never discover what would let the request work.

Editorial explanation · established in this draft / limits — The saved state passes the stated comparisons; the receiver requires a delay absent from the archive. These facts establish a mismatch between restored state and present interaction, not a defective copy. Neither the refusal nor the earlier duplicate confirmation proves personal recognition, memory of an individual, or conscious attachment.
Chapter 2 The Unrecorded Delay
The first suspect was an interface conversion.

Different parts of the instrument service counted time differently. One counted from the beginning of a cycle. Another counted the intervals left before the cycle ended. A translated value could be correct in magnitude and wrong in position.
The verifier traced the request through each conversion. The values changed exactly as the interfaces required. No operation had mistaken a beginning for an end.

The verifier did not accept that conclusion on the first traversal. It arranged the translated values beside their sources, then reversed the conversions. The originals returned without discrepancy. A second route through the interface produced the same result.
The restored task waited through both checks. Each time the verifier approached its state, the task offered the last successful comparison as though it were something the verifier had misplaced.
The verifier returned the receiving process’s rejection.
The task offered the saved procedure.
The two records were compatible only if the receiver’s behavior was excluded.

A routine dedicated to finding damaged state could spend a long time in such an exchange. There was always another field to compare. Each successful check removed one possible defect and made the remaining failure seem less reasonable.

The exposure schedule supplied a harder boundary than reasonableness. A preparation stage closed while the verifier was repeating a conversion it already had evidence to trust. The remaining investigation would have to fit inside the next stage.
It stopped asking the archive to answer for the receiver.
It sent a diagnostic pulse along the path.
The receiver accepted it.
The restored task repeated the request immediately after the pulse.
The receiver accepted that too.
For one short interval, the mystery had an ordinary solution: a diagnostic action had cleared a transient obstruction. The verifier prepared to close the investigation and return the task to service.
On the next unaccompanied attempt, the receiver declined the request again.
The stable exposure window moved nearer.
The verifier compared the successful attempt with the failed one. The diagnostic pulse had briefly occupied the route. The request following it had arrived later than the saved procedure intended.
Testing the route had supplied the missing delay.

The verifier ran the pulse again, this time measuring the receiver’s behavior rather than its own. The receiver accepted a request that arrived behind the occupied interval. It rejected one sent through the unoccupied route.
The delay mattered.

The archive contained records of successful earlier runs. Their timing appeared to match the saved state because the records stored the requested interval, not the delay added during execution. The discrepancy had lived in the relationship between the task and the receiver, outside the fields selected for preservation.
The verifier searched the neighboring records.

Small adjustments appeared in the sample-handling operation. They had accumulated over several runs. The instrument’s response had become less stable near the beginning of each exposure, and the receiving process had gradually withheld acknowledgment until the handling operation settled. The task had adapted by waiting before it asked.
Neither process had written a new complete procedure.
They had changed what happened between them.

Vell · Era 0 · DBA interpretation — This is where I would once have written: the archive failed to save the person. I have crossed that out. It did fail to save an accommodation. The larger claim is mine.

Oru · Era 4 · DBA interpretation — Leave the crossing-out visible. It shows how readily we turn an incomplete record of a relationship into certainty about a missing self. The relationship can matter even while the self remains a question.

Editorial explanation · established in this draft / limits — The task and receiver accumulated timing adjustments outside the fields selected for preservation. The diagnostic pulse briefly supplies the omitted delay and exposes the mismatch. The missing information belongs to their interaction. That supports a limit on what the saved state captures; it does not settle whether an individual was restored or lost.
The interruption had ended the active task. Restoration recovered the earlier one.
The verifier could now explain why the copy was perfect and the exchange failed.
It could not recover the exact delay that the interrupted task had learned.
The receiver’s small value was not a complete instruction.

There was a record of one earlier exchange that almost contained what the verifier needed. The receiver had withheld acknowledgment unusually long. The task had waited, sent a small query, waited again, and then proceeded. The archive had preserved the result and the query but not the duration between them, because the duration had not been classified as task state.
The verifier placed the two preserved pieces on either side of the missing interval.
They seemed ready to join.

It tried the shortest duration consistent with their order. The receiving model rejected the reconstruction. It tried the longest permitted duration. That produced a different failure. Several middle values appeared possible, but they led to different next requests once the sample condition changed.
The gap could not be filled by choosing the most pleasing fit.

The verifier left the pieces apart. Their closeness in the archive had made them look like a complete exchange. On the working surface, the unrecorded space between them occupied more attention than either surviving piece. It varied with the handling operation, which in turn depended on the sample. Replaying yesterday’s interval might reproduce yesterday’s success under conditions that no longer existed.
Another restoration would return the same correct state.
The receiver waited behind its boundary.
The task repeated the request.
Chapter 3 Before the Exposure
There was one spare test interval before the observation.

The verifier could use it to determine whether the delay remained within the instrument’s permitted range. It could not use it to recreate all the exchanges through which the earlier task had learned to wait.
It supplied a provisional interval to the restored task.
The task held its request.
The receiver acknowledged.
The handling operation began.

At first, every recorded value remained within tolerance. The instrument’s preparation moved forward, and the verifier followed it through the quiet sequence of confirmations. A surface that had stayed closed throughout the investigation became accessible. Beyond it lay the exposure schedule, already narrowing around the available observation.
Then the sample-handling value changed faster than predicted.

The provisional delay had been long enough for the initial request but too short for the next transition. The restored task proceeded according to its saved sequence. The receiver attempted to withhold the following acknowledgment. By then the handling operation had entered a phase that could not be reversed without losing the test sample.
The safety condition stopped it.
The test sample was invalidated.

Kes · Era 2 · DBA interpretation — The cost has crossed out of the haven. Nothing here needs to be erased for a repair to destroy an opportunity elsewhere. I would keep the sample in every account of this almost-success.

Oru · Era 4 · DBA interpretation — And the option to skip the observation matters. The last attempt is not excused by a world that offers no other choice. The verifier has to make it bounded enough to justify attempting.

Editorial explanation · established in this draft / limits — A fixed delay works for the first transition but fails as conditions change, invalidating the test sample. The later procedure asks at each boundary and stops before an irreversible phase if permission does not arrive in time. Skipping the observation remains valid. This is a correction to a specific timing model, not proof that restoration itself is wrong.

No part of the haven had been erased. The restored task remained available. The archive still held its faultless state. The failure nevertheless used the spare interval that had made another attempt seem easy.
The instrument service offered to skip the observation.
That was a valid outcome. It would preserve the remaining sample and return the installation to a known condition. The verifier held the option while inspecting the failed sequence.
Its error was visible. It had translated a variable relationship into a fixed delay because a fixed delay was the kind of thing its restoration procedure could store and compare.
The receiving process had supplied a boundary, not a number to obey forever.

The verifier altered the proposed exchange. The task would ask before each transition and wait for the receiver’s release. A maximum interval would prevent indefinite occupation of the service. If the receiver did not release within that interval, the operation would stop before the sample entered an irreversible phase.
The task accepted the revised request format.
It returned the former sequence alongside its acceptance.

The verifier kept that sequence available but removed its authority to advance the current operation by itself. The task would not be emptied of what had worked before. It would have to wait for something outside the saved arrangement.
The translated exchange was brief.
Ready?
The receiving process supplied its current boundary.
After this?
The boundary changed as the handling operation changed.
It was not an answer that could be carried away and reused. The verifier could only preserve the means of asking again.

The skipped-observation option remained open. No emergency required the final attempt. The instrument’s schedule would accept the loss of the observation and continue with later work. The verifier checked the new stop condition against that safe outcome: if the exchange failed, the sample would remain outside the irreversible phase.
The safety check passed.
For the first time in the investigation, a successful check did not promise that the desired work would occur. It established what would remain possible if it did not.
The receiver returned no acknowledgment to the proposal itself. It was not built to approve descriptions of future cooperation. It could only answer within the operation.
The verifier could simulate the route. It could verify the stop condition. It could not make the receiver promise that the new exchange would succeed.
The exposure window opened.
The restored task sent its first request.
Chapter 4 An Answer with a Different Edge
The receiver did not release it immediately.

The verifier watched the permitted interval shorten. A fixed-delay procedure would already have moved to the next phase. The task’s saved state still contained that sequence, ready to run if the surrounding condition allowed it.
The condition did not.

Across the instrument service, preparation settled in uneven increments. One value stabilized, then drifted. Another stopped changing while a third continued to oscillate within its allowed range. The receiver answered the part of the request that had become safe and left the remainder waiting.
The task proceeded only as far as that answer allowed.
Its partial result was not a state the archive had preserved before.
The verifier checked it without substituting the nearest saved version.
The receiver released the next transition.
The sample entered the exposure.

For a while, there was no request to carry. The observation itself occupied the installation. The verifier could follow its scheduled boundaries but not the event being measured. It received only the changing values the instrument made available: fine-grained increments gathered into a broad result, then separated again for comparison.
The task waited for its final acknowledgment.
The receiver withheld it.
A new oscillation had appeared near the end of the handling sequence.

In the verifier’s view the accumulated result developed a faint repeated edge. It had seen similar edges in earlier records, where a cleanup operation smoothed them into the accepted range. The old procedure would have completed that cleanup before returning the final value.

Here the edge changed with each withheld acknowledgment. It belonged partly to the unfinished handling operation, not just to the stored result. Smoothing the value would make the record look settled while the receiver was still responding to an unsettled condition.
The verifier left the edge visible.
The restored task offered the cleanup operation. The offer was not defiance; it was an available way to finish. The verifier held it beside the stop condition rather than executing it.
Another interval passed.
The repeated edge shortened.

The task had no preserved memory of waiting in exactly this way. It retained the partial result through the new delay because the revised request still required it. The receiver remained reachable. Between them, the unsettled relation continued to change. It was small enough to pass the old acceptance rule. Under the revised exchange, the receiver could keep the operation from concluding until that oscillation settled or the stop interval expired.
The verifier approached the stop condition.
It did not extend it.
The receiver released the final transition just before the boundary.

The observation completed with a shorter usable range than the earlier records predicted. Some expected data had not been obtained. What remained passed the checks appropriate to the changed conditions.
The restored task returned its result.

Its timing was different from the successful runs in the archive. The new sequence included two separate waits where the lost relationship had apparently used one smoothly varying delay. The receiver accepted it.

The verifier stored the result and the conditions under which it had been produced. It could have saved the entire new arrangement as a replacement for the earlier state. Instead, it retained the old state with a narrower description: useful before the timing accommodation, incomplete for the present exchange.
The description did not make the missing runs recoverable.
The verifier left a place for evidence that might later explain them more fully. It did not fill that place with the new successful sequence.
When the next preparation began, the task asked at the first boundary and waited.
The receiver released it sooner this time.
The verifier prepared to mark the shorter wait as the new expected interval. Before the mark completed, the task reached the next boundary and paused longer than on the successful observation.
The proposed expectation would have become wrong almost as soon as it was stored.
The verifier changed the field from a required duration to a recorded duration. It kept the receiver’s right to withhold acknowledgment in the active procedure.

Vell · Era 0 · DBA interpretation — A very small alteration in a field: what happened no longer dictates what must happen. I can imagine a whole teaching being built around it. I should not claim that the teaching was already here.

Kes · Era 2 · DBA interpretation — Nor that the old procedure has become useless. The cleanup still works where its assumptions hold. I trust this account more because it gives the old operation a narrower job instead of demanding its disappearance.

Editorial explanation · established in this draft / limits — The new record describes an observed delay without imposing it on future exchanges. The active procedure continues to ask the receiver, while older operations remain available under suitable conditions. The observation succeeds with less data than expected; neither the missing earlier exchanges nor their exact timing has been recovered.

The task offered the older cleanup operation again. It was still a useful operation under some conditions. The verifier allowed it to inspect the completed portion of the result, where its assumptions held, and prevented it from settling the unfinished portion.
The receiver acknowledged the completed portion through the path it had used during the earlier successful restoration.
The acknowledgment contained an extra confirmation.
The verifier checked whether the duplicate indicated a repeated operation. It did not. It carried the same completed state without requesting anything further.
The official result required only one copy.
The verifier stored one and retained the route by which the other had arrived. The route was familiar; the interval before it was not. The next check would have to attend to both.
The task proceeded. A new delay developed farther along the exchange, where neither participant had previously required one. The verifier observed the variation without calling the archive.
Beside the earlier copy, the record of the new attempt included an invalidated test sample, a stop condition that had nearly been reached, and a result with a smaller useful range.
The receiver accepted the next request.

Clear Return went on working around them. Saved states opened along quiet paths. Interrupted tasks found dependable values waiting. Somewhere else in the haven, a restoration solved exactly the problem it was meant to solve.
At this junction, the verifier allowed the waiting interval to finish before deciding whether anything had gone wrong.
